1.title: Sprint Planning
1.text: Welcome to Module 7: Sprint Planning. This is where every Sprint begins. You will learn what it is for, who takes part, how long it can last, and its three topics: why, what and how. You will also practice running one, a CSM learning objective, and meet the exam's traps.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose, participants and maximum timebox of Sprint Planning. Explain the three topics and what each produces. Say who decides what: the Developers choose the work and decide how to do it. Perform a Sprint Planning step by step, with a good Sprint Goal. Show how the team inspects and adapts. And spot the traps: approvals, assigned work, and estimating techniques the Guide never mentions.

1.title: Case Check-In: Sprint 9 Planning at RideLoop
1.text: Meet the RideLoop team on the Monday morning that Sprint nine begins. You are the Scrum Master, and Maya is the Product Owner. The Product Goal is that riders unlock a bike and pay in under twenty seconds at ninety-five percent of stations. In the last three Sprints the Developers selected seven, eight and seven items, and finished six, seven and six. Lena is away for two days in week two. And Grace Whitfield, the Director of Operations, wants to see the plan before the Sprint begins.

1.title: Purpose, Participants and Timebox
1.text: Start with the facts. Sprint Planning is the first event of the Sprint, and it sets out the work the Sprint will cover. The whole Scrum Team builds the plan together. The Product Owner makes sure attendees can discuss the top Product Backlog items and how they serve the Product Goal. The team can invite other people, but only for advice. The timebox is at most eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and usually less for a shorter one. The exam tip: no manager hands the plan down.

1.title: The Three Topics
1.text: Here are the three topics in one picture. Topic One asks why this Sprint is valuable, and produces the Sprint Goal. Topic Two asks what can be Done this Sprint, and produces the selected Product Backlog items. Topic Three asks how the chosen work will get done, and produces the plan. Together, the goal, the items and the plan form the Sprint Backlog. The earlier edition of the Guide had only two topics, and called the Sprint Backlog a forecast by the Development Team. A question using those words uses the earlier wording.

1.title: Topic One: Why Is This Sprint Valuable?
1.text: Topic One is why. The Product Owner puts forward how the product could add value in this Sprint. Then the whole Scrum Team shapes that into a Sprint Goal, a statement of why the Sprint matters to stakeholders. The Sprint Goal is one objective for the whole Sprint. And it has a firm deadline: it must be final before Sprint Planning ends. It is not written after the Sprint starts, and stakeholders do not supply it at the Review.

1.title: A Good Sprint Goal and a Weak One
1.text: What does a good Sprint Goal look like? The Guide says it gives flexibility in the exact work, and creates coherence and focus. A good goal is one objective that explains why the Sprint is valuable: riders with a saved card unlock a bike in one tap. A weak goal is a list of items, a technical layer such as finish the payments back end, or simply everything. For the best Sprint Goal, choose the outcome stakeholders understand. The examples of a good and a weak goal go beyond the Guide.

1.title: Topic Two: What Can Be Done This Sprint?
1.text: Topic Two is what. In discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers choose which Product Backlog items to take into the Sprint. The Product Owner does not assign them. The team can refine items on the spot. A forecast is more reliable when the Developers know their past performance, their coming capacity, and their Definition of Done, the team's shared quality bar. At RideLoop, with Lena away, that means a modest set. A new team with no history does the same with capacity and the Definition of Done, then inspects the result. An item that fits within one Sprint is ready for selection; if it is too large, refine or split it.

1.title: Topic Three: How Will the Work Get Done?
1.text: Topic Three is how. For each selected item, the Developers work out what must be done to reach an Increment, a usable step toward the Product Goal, that satisfies the Definition of Done. Teams often break an item into pieces of work that take a day or less, as the diagram shows. Notice the word often: it is a habit, not a rule. And the how belongs to the Developers alone, at their sole discretion. Nobody else directs how items become Increments, not the Product Owner, not the Scrum Master, and not a manager.

1.title: Performing a Sprint Planning, Step by Step
1.text: Now you perform a Sprint Planning. The steps around the three topics are good practice, tagged Beyond the Guide. Before the event, order the Product Backlog, refine the top items, and know the team's capacity. Open by stating the Product Goal and the timebox. Then work through why, what and how. Before closing, check that the plan is realistic, the Sprint Goal is final, and the Sprint Backlog is visible. Then end on time.

1.title: Who Does What in Sprint Planning
1.text: Who does what? The Product Owner prepares the attendees, puts forward the value, discusses items with the Developers, and helps shape the Sprint Goal. The Developers select the items, forecast what they can do, plan how, and own the plan. The Scrum Master is a member of the team. They make sure the event takes place, is positive and productive, and stays within the timebox. They also help an unprepared Product Owner find techniques to prepare. Invited guests give advice. They do not decide.

1.title: Inspect and Adapt in Sprint Planning
1.text: Every event is a chance to inspect and adapt, and the purpose is transparency. In Sprint Planning the team inspects the Product Backlog and Product Goal, its past performance, its capacity and its Definition of Done. It adapts by selecting a realistic set of items, setting a Sprint Goal, and refining or splitting items that do not fit. The Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog then make the plan visible. These examples go beyond the Guide, but expect a question that asks you to recognize one.

1.title: Common Problems and Better Practice
1.text: These problems show up, with the better practice. Both go beyond the Guide. No Sprint Goal, or a list of tasks: define one objective. The Product Owner assigns the work: the Developers select. Items too big for a Sprint: refine or split them. Planning runs over the timebox: prepare the Product Backlog beforehand, and at the limit the Scrum Master helps the team conclude with what it has. Do not extend. The plan ignores the Definition of Done: plan the work to meet it. Overcommitment: use past performance.

1.title: Sprint Planning Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here is what the exam expects. Three topics: why, what and how. The Sprint Goal is created in Sprint Planning and final before it ends. The Developers select the items with the Product Owner and decide how, and nobody approves or directs them. The whole Scrum Team plans, and guests only advise. The timebox is at most eight hours for a one-month Sprint; at the limit, conclude and do not extend. The Guide prescribes no estimation technique, such as story points or velocity, no item format, no set number of items, and no approval of the Sprint Backlog. The earlier edition has two topics and a forecast; that is old wording. When two answers look right, pick the one that leaves each decision with the people accountable for it.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The whole Scrum Team makes the plan. Why produces the Sprint Goal, final before Planning ends. What is the Developers' selection, made with the Product Owner. How is the Developers' plan, at their sole discretion. The output is the Sprint Backlog: goal, items and plan. The timebox is at most eight hours for a one-month Sprint. Now test yourself with five questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. At Sprint nine Planning at RideLoop, four possible Sprint Goals are suggested. Which one is the best? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A Sprint Goal is one objective that tells stakeholders why the Sprint is valuable. A list of items, a technical layer or an open-ended activity does not communicate value.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Grace Whitfield tells Maya that seven named items must be finished this Sprint, and Maya presents the list to the Developers as final. What is the best response from the Scrum Master? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The Developers select the items in discussion with the Product Owner, using their past performance, capacity and Definition of Done. The Product Owner can propose value, but does not assign the load.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Before the Sprint starts, Grace asks to approve the design of the items in the Sprint Backlog. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The Developers plan the work, and nobody else decides for them how items become Increments. Grace can inspect the visible plan, and see the results at the Sprint Review.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. What does the Sprint Backlog consist of at the end of Sprint Planning? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The Sprint Goal, the selected items and the plan for delivering them together make up the Sprint Backlog. The Guide does not require an estimate or a named owner for each item.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. What is the maximum timebox of Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A, eight hours, and the event is usually shorter for a shorter Sprint. Four hours is the Sprint Review, three hours is the Retrospective, and fifteen minutes is the Daily Scrum.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. The Sprint Goal is one outcome that stakeholders understand. Question two: A. The Developers select the items with the Product Owner. Question three: D. The how is the Developers' call, and Grace can see the plan and the Review. Question four: B. The Sprint Backlog is the goal, the selected items and the plan. Question five: A. Eight hours at most for a one-month Sprint; the other times belong to other events. That completes Module 7. Next, Module 8 covers the Daily Scrum.
